extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and examiner/practitioner guidance for when and how U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and certain international application publications are available as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), and methods to overcome rejections based on such references.

rubrics_metrics.name: When there is no common assignee, applicant, or inventor, earlier U.S. application must issue or be published before being prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no common assignee, common applicant, or common inventor and the application was not published pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 122(b), the confidential status of applications under 35 U.S.C. 122(a) must be maintained and no rejection can be made relying on the earlier filed, unpublished application, or subject matter not supported in a redacted application publication, as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier-filed application will not be published pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 122(b), it must be allowed to issue once statutory requirements are met; after issuance it may be used as a reference in a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection against a still-pending application. For applications subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g), interferences may be proper when filing dates are within 6 months (3 months for simple subject matter). See MPEP § 2136.02 and § 2136 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: When common assignee/applicant/inventor exists, provisional pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to provisionally reject a later application over an earlier filed, and unpublished, application under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) when there is a common assignee, applicant, or inventor. A provisional rejection may also be made if the earlier filed copending U.S. application has been published as redacted (37 CFR 1.217) and the subject matter relied upon in the rejection is not supported in the redacted publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional rejections put applicant on notice early and give opportunity to overcome by amendment or evidence; more options are available when applications have same assignee. Provisional rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) are only authorized when there is a common inventor or assignee. Use form paragraph 7.15.01.fti when making such provisional rejection. See In re Irish, Ex parte Bartfeld and MPEP § 2136.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) / CREATE Act limitations on applying 102(e) prior art in obviousness rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c), as amended by the CREATE Act, continues to apply only to subject matter which qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g), and which is being relied upon in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103. It does not apply to subject matter applied in a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or a double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A provisional rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) using prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is not proper if the application contains evidence that the application and the prior art reference were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made. Certain non-commonly owned references may be disqualified under the CREATE Act. See MPEP §§ 2146-2146.03 for details on disqualification and evidence of common ownership or joint research agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: A 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection may rely on any part of the patent or application publication disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the entire disclosure of a U.S. patent, a U.S. patent application publication, or an international application publication having an earlier effective U.S. filing date can be relied on to reject the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Sun Studs, Inc. v. ATA Equip. Leasing, Inc., and MPEP § 2120.01 for authority. Examiner should consider the full disclosure of the reference when formulating anticipation or obviousness grounds using a 102(e) reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference itself must contain the subject matter relied on in the rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or an international application publication is used to reject claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the disclosure relied on in the rejection must be present in the issued patent or application publication; subject matter not included cannot be relied on as of the reference's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portions canceled in prosecution are not part of the patent/publication and cannot be relied on (Ex parte Stalego). Subject matter disclosed only in an abandoned, unpublished parent that was not carried into the child patent/publication may not be relied on (In re Klesper). For CIPs, subject matter in parent but not included in the CIP cannot be relied on as prior art of the CIP (In re Lund). When a patent claims benefit to a provisional, at least one claim of the patent must be supported by the provisional in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 to use the provisional filing date. See MPEP § 2136.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority date cannot be used as the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) reference date
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is explicitly limited to certain references 'filed in the United States before the invention thereof by the applicant.' Foreign applications' filing dates claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119 or 365(a) cannot be used as pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) dates for prior art purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection by proving entitlement to a U.S. priority date (35 U.S.C. 119) earlier than the reference's U.S. filing date; see In re Hilmer and MPEP § 216 for procedures considering applicant's right of priority. Certain PCT filings (meeting specific conditions) may be treated as U.S. filings—see MPEP § 2120.01 and related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: International (PCT) application filed on or after Nov 29, 2000: three conditions to treat international filing date as U.S. filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: If the international application (A) has an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000; (B) designated the United States; and (C) was published under PCT Article 21(2) in English, then the international filing date is a U.S. filing date for prior art purposes under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such an international application properly claims benefit to an earlier U.S. or international application, apply the reference as of the earlier filing date provided the conditions of 102(e) and 35 U.S.C. 120 or 365(c) are met and the relied-upon subject matter is disclosed in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If the international application did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English, do not treat the international filing date as a U.S. filing date; apply the reference instead under 102(a)/(b) as of publication or as of any later U.S. filing date that properly claims the benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: International applications filed before Nov 29, 2000 are subject to former 102(e) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: References based on international applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 are to be applied under the pre-AIPA version of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (i.e., as in force on November 28, 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply U.S. patents under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as of the earlier of completion of 371(c)(1),(2) and (4) requirements or the filing date of the later-filed U.S. application that claimed benefit; U.S. application and WIPO publications directly resulting from international applications under PCT Article 21(2) are never applied under the former 102(e) but may be applied under pre-AIA 102(a) or (b) as of publication; see MPEP § 2136.03 subsections for detailed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) requires written description support
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical reference date of a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or international application publication having prior art effect under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) may be the filing date of a relied-upon provisional application only if at least one claim of the reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dynamic Drinkware and Amgen v. Sanofi cited. The provisional must describe the subject matter relied upon in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112; see MPEP § 2136 examples for illustration. International applications that (1) were filed before Nov 29, 2000, (2) did not designate the U.S., or (3) were not published in English cannot be used to reach back via priority for pre-AIA 102(e) purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 120 requires support in the earlier-filed application
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent or patent application publication that claims the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 (continuation, divisional, CIP) will be accorded the earlier filing date as its prior art date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), provided the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier-filed application does not support the relied-upon subject matter, the earlier filing date cannot be used to antedate the reference. See MPEP § 2136 examples 2 and 5–9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date is the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) reference date (not conception or reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reference available under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) discloses but does not claim the subject matter of the claims being examined or an obvious variant, the reference is not prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g). The effective date of the reference as prior art is its filing date in the United States; the date that the prior art subject matter was conceived or reduced to practice is of no importance when pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is not at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception or reduction to practice only becomes an issue when 102(g) (interference) is in play. See Sun Studs v. ATA Equip. Leasing and MPEP §§ 2120.01 and 2136 for examples (e.g., Mouat/Mason & Sohn case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'by another' / different inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Another' means other than applicants; in other words, a different inventive entity. The inventive entity is different if not all inventors are the same. The fact that the application and reference have one or more inventors in common is immaterial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A different inventive entity is prima facie evidence that the reference is 'by another' (Milburn rule). Even if some inventors overlap, the reference to a patent or application by a different inventive entity indicates applicant was not first inventor. See In re Land, Ex parte DesOrmeaux, In re Mathews, and MPEP § 2136.04–.05 for methods to overcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (A–F)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing reference is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention (when appropriate); (E) submitting and perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); and/or (F) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and establishing the prior application satisfies enablement/written description requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2133.02(a), 715–716, 2136.05(a) and (b) for procedural requirements and examples. Note: a terminal disclaimer does not overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection. If the rejection is the only possible ground and there is no common assignee or inventor, the examiner must consider whether an interference should be declared (MPEP Chapter 2300).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antedating a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) reference via 37 CFR 1.131 or priority/benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection can be overcome by antedating the filing date of the reference by submitting an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 proving prior invention, or by establishing priority/benefit to an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119 or 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavits can prove invention prior to the reference's effective date, but are not acceptable if the claims of the reference and application are directed to the same invention or obvious variants—in such cases double patenting or interference may be appropriate. See MPEP §§ 715, 2136.05(a). Priority/benefit claims must be timely (see 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.78), and applicant must show the earlier application satisfies enablement and written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 112). Details differ for applications filed on/after vs prior to September 16, 2012 (use of corrected ADS, ADS or oath/declaration). Certified priority documents and translations may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 vs 1.132: appropriate uses and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by proving invention prior to the effective date of the reference. An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 is used when the reference is inventor's or a joint inventor's own work (i.e., to show reference is not 'by another').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1.131 is not appropriate if the reference describes an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work; in that case submit 1.132. A 1.131 cannot be used when claims are directed to the same invention or obvious variants—then consider double patenting or interference. A naked assertion of inventorship under 1.132 without context, explanation, or supporting evidence is insufficient (EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen). See MPEP §§ 715, 716, 2136.05(a)–(b) for required contents and permitted situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing priority/benefit requirements and timing (37 CFR 1.55, 1.78; ADS/Oath differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: To antedate a reference via priority (35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d)) or benefit (35 U.S.C. 119(e)/120) claims, applicant must submit the claim within the time periods set in 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 and establish that the prior foreign or prior U.S. application satisfies enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (for post-Sep 16, 2012) or pre-AIA 112 first paragraph (for earlier filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications filed on/after Sep 16, 2012, identify prior applications via a corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76; for earlier applications identify in the oath/declaration or ADS per 37 CFR 1.63/1.76. The foreign priority filing date must antedate the reference and be perfected (certified priority document and English translation required if not in English). Grantable petitions exist for unintentionally delayed priority/benefit claims. See MPEP §§ 213–216 and 2136.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing reference is inventor's own work (37 CFR 1.132) requires substantive evidence, not naked assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the reference invention is not by 'another' (i.e., it is the inventor's or a joint inventor's own work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue turns on what the evidence of record shows as to who invented the subject matter. A declaration that is only a bare assertion of inventorship without context, explanation, or supporting evidence is insufficient (see EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen). Provide corroborating details, explanation, and evidence to lend credence to inventorship assertions. See MPEP § 2136.05(b) and MPEP §§ 715–716 for required contents.
